title: The Environments of Luminous Fast Blue Optical Transients: Evidence for a Compact Object and Wolf-Rayet Star Merger Origin
comment: 32 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a comprehensive analysis of the host galaxies of 11 luminous fast blue optical transients (LFBOTs). We model new and archival host photometry and spectroscopy with Prospector. We determine that all LFBOT hosts are actively star-forming with recent bursts of star formation and have a median stellar mass of $\log(M_*/M_\odot)=9.61^{+0.74}_{-1.61}$, present-day star formation rate SFR=$0.95^{+18.37}_{-0.91} M_\odot$yr$^{-1}$, and gas-phase oxygen abundance metallicity 12+log(O/H)=$8.71^{+0.17}_{-0.40}$. To contextualize these results, we compare them to the host properties of Hydrogen-poor superluminous supernovae (SLSNe-I), several core-collapse supernova subtypes (CCSN; SNe Ibc, II, and Ibn) and long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs). We find that LFBOT hosts are more star-forming than CCSN hosts, but less star-forming than SLSN-I hosts. We further show that LFBOT hosts are more metal-poor than SN Ibc and II hosts, but more metal-rich than SLSN-I and LGRB hosts. Finally, we find that, similar to SLSNe-I and unlike CCSNe and LGRBs, a large fraction (>30%) of LFBOTs occur in their hosts' faintest pixel or outside their host galaxy's light. Our results indicate that LFBOTs have massive stellar origin that do not trace active star-forming regions within their hosts and have a weaker metallicity-dependence than other extreme transients. For these reasons, we favor a compact-object and Wolf-Rayet star merger progenitor scenario. Future discoveries of LFBOTs with the Rubin observatory will help to increase their sample size and place firmer constraints on their environments and progenitors.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 11 LFBOT host galaxies, finding they are moderately star-forming and metal-rich compared to some other explosive transients. Their unique host properties and locations suggest LFBOTs stem from massive star mergers rather than typical core-collapse events.
AI.motivation: To understand the nature and progenitors of luminous fast blue optical transients (LFBOTs) by studying their host galaxy properties.
AI.method: Modeling of new and archival photometry and spectroscopy of 11 LFBOT host galaxies using Prospector, with comparison to host properties of other transient types (SLSNe-I, CCSNe subtypes, LGRBs).
AI.result: LFBOT hosts are actively star-forming with recent bursts, have intermediate stellar masses and metallicities, more star-forming than CCSN hosts but less than SLSN-I hosts, and display a unique spatial distribution within their hosts. They show weaker metallicity dependence and often occur in faint or outer regions of their hosts.
AI.conclusion: LFBOTs likely originate from massive stars but do not trace active star-forming regions strongly; their environments support a progenitor scenario involving compact-object and Wolf-Rayet star mergers. Future observations will refine these constraints.

title: Radiation-ionization hydrodynamic simulations of AGN line-driven winds lead to transient shielding and BAL/UFO signatures
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS, 17 pages, 12 figures and 7 videos as supplementary material on MNRAS website
summary: Disc winds from active galactic nuclei (AGN) can be launched by radiation pressure acting on spectral lines. However, launching a line-driven wind in the X-ray rich environment of AGN is challenging, as the wind easily gets over-ionized. Previous simulations suggested that X-ray self-shielding could enable line driving, though it remained unclear whether this relied on simplified treatments of radiation and ionization. Here, we revisit the X-ray shielding scenario using the first multi-frequency, multi-directional Monte-Carlo radiative photo-ionization hydrodynamical simulations of AGN line-driven winds. We find that sustaining a steady wind with mass-loss rates of $\approx20\%$ of the accretion rate requires an unrealistically weak X-ray flux ($α_{\rm OX}<-3$). For stronger X-ray emission ($-3<α_{\rm OX}<-1$), self-shielding is only transient, leading to episodic ejections with mass-loss rates approaching the accretion rate. Our steady winds naturally produce FeLoBAL, HiBAL, and broad emission line signatures, depending on the disc spectral energy distribution and the observer's inclination. At moderate X-ray luminosities ($α_{\rm OX}\sim-3$), transient winds can generate short-lived BAL and ultra-fast outflow (UFO) features. At the highest X-ray luminosities ($α_{\rm OX}\sim-1$), the winds are too ionized to form BALs, but still produce UFOs. These results imply that additional physics is required to explain BAL outflows at realistic X-ray levels and to drive winds strong enough for AGN feedback. Nonetheless, our simulations provide a new framework for interpreting the observed diversity of AGN outflow signatures with fully coupled radiation and dynamics.

AI.tldr: This study uses detailed radiative hydrodynamical simulations to show that line-driven winds in AGN face strong challenges from X-ray ionization, producing only transient or weak winds at realistic X-ray levels, suggesting that additional mechanisms are necessary to explain observed AGN outflows.
AI.motivation: To understand the viability of line-driven disc winds in the high X-ray radiation environment of AGN, and to clarify the role of X-ray self-shielding in enabling such winds with more accurate simulations.
AI.method: Conducting multi-frequency, multi-directional Monte-Carlo radiative photo-ionization hydrodynamical simulations of AGN line-driven winds to accurately model radiation, ionization, and wind dynamics.
AI.result: Found that steady line-driven winds require unrealistically weak X-ray flux; transient self-shielding can produce episodic ejections with high mass-loss rates; different wind properties and observational signatures depend on X-ray luminosity and disc spectral energy distribution.
AI.conclusion: Line-driven winds alone cannot explain strong BAL outflows under realistic X-ray emission levels, indicating the need for additional physics to account for AGN feedback-strength winds. The simulations provide a comprehensive framework linking AGN outflow signatures to radiation and dynamics.

title: IXPE view of the Crab pulsar following the 17 July and 6 August 2025 glitches
comment: 15 pages, 5 tables, 7 figures accepted for publication in Astrophysical Journal on 24 March 2026
summary: The Crab pulsar experienced two relatively small glitches separated by only 20 days in September and October 2025. IXPE observed the source twice, with delay times since the glitch epoch ranging between 35 and 75 days, depending on the observation. We carried out a multi-method analysis to investigate whether there is evidence for significant changes in the polarization properties of the pulsar, underlying possible variations in the pulsar magnetosphere itself following the glitches. Specifically, we performed: (1) phase-averaged polarimetry of the Crab pulsar before and after the glitches, following an approach similar to that adopted in 2019 by PolarLight, a non-imaging CubeSat-class photoelectric polarimeter which observed a change in the X-ray polarization within 100 days after a stronger glitch in July 2019; (2) a comparison, before and after the glitch, of phase-resolved X-ray polarimetry with IXPE, not possible with PolarLight. Furthermore, we investigated, by means of phase-resolved optical (OPTIMA) polarimetry, whether a significant change in the X-to-optical lag was present in the data before and after the glitch. We find no evidence of a change in the polarization for the pulsar emission before and after the glitch, We use the upper limits obtained to estimate the maximum change in magnetic obliquity allowed by the data, using the standard rotating vector model and assuming that the glitch is due to a neutron-star quake. We constrain this maximum change to be no greater than $\pm4^{o}$ at the 95\% confidence level.

AI.tldr: Analyzing Crab pulsar polarization before and after 2025 glitches using IXPE and optical data reveals no significant change, placing stringent limits on magnetospheric geometry variations post-glitch.
AI.motivation: To investigate potential changes in the Crab pulsar's magnetosphere following glitches, motivated by previous observations of polarization changes after a stronger glitch in 2019.
AI.method: Conducted a multi-method analysis including phase-averaged X-ray polarimetry before and after two small glitches using IXPE, phase-resolved X-ray polarimetry comparison, and phase-resolved optical polarimetry to check for changes in X-to-optical lag.
AI.result: No significant changes in polarization properties were found following the glitches; upper limits on magnetic obliquity change constrained to ±4 degrees at 95% confidence assuming a neutron-star quake origin for the glitch.
AI.conclusion: The study finds no detectable variation in polarization related to the Crab pulsar glitches of 2025, thereby limiting possible magnetospheric or geometric changes caused by these glitches to small angles within ±4 degrees.

title: Near-Infrared and Optical Observations of SN 2024rbc: The First Early Detection of CO and Dust in a Type Ib Supernova
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures, 5 tables; Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present optical and near-infrared (NIR) observations of the Type Ib supernova (SN) 2024rbc. Emission from the first CO overtone, resting on a dust continuum at $2.3-2.4$ $μ$m, was observed at 62 days post-explosion. The CO band heads are not seen; the emission is broad and devoid of sharp spectral structure. This is the first observation of CO in the ejecta of a Type Ib SN reported in literature. Fitting a LTE model to the CO overtone derives a mass of $(5.2 \pm 1.2)$ $\times$ 10$^{-4}$ $M_{\odot}$, a temperature of $4040 \pm 435$ K, and a velocity of $5905 \pm 1960$ km s$^{-1}$. We also fitted a modified blackbody model to the dust continuum, deriving a dust temperature of $910 \pm 10$ K and a mass of $(1.3 \pm 0.1)$ $\times$ $10^{-3}$ $M_{\odot}$. Furthermore, the spectra of SN 2024rbc exhibit strong He I lines and numerous neutral and ionized metal lines. Comparing the spectral evolution of SN 2024rbc to other Type Ib, Ic, and IIb SNe indicates it is a Type Ib SN. Additionally, fitting SN light curve models of helium star progenitors computed with the STELLA code to photometric observations indicates a $^{56}$Ni mass of $0.07$ $M_\odot$ and an ejecta mass of $1.7$ $M_\odot$. We also compare the velocities of key optical lines to examine the evolution of the ejecta. Lastly, we discuss the observed CO and dust emission and its implications for early-Universe dust formation.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the first observation of CO emission in a Type Ib supernova (SN 2024rbc) ejecta, derives physical parameters of the CO and dust, confirms the SN type through spectral and photometric analysis, and discusses the implications for dust formation in the early Universe.
AI.motivation: To investigate molecular and dust formation in the ejecta of a Type Ib supernova, specifically the first reported CO emission in such an event, and to better understand the progenitor characteristics and the implications for early-Universe dust formation.
AI.method: Optical and near-infrared spectroscopic observations were conducted on SN 2024rbc, followed by LTE modeling of the CO overtone band, modified blackbody fitting of the dust continuum, spectral line identification and velocity measurements, spectral evolution comparisons with other SNe types, and fitting of light curve models using the STELLA code.
AI.result: Detection of CO first overtone emission at 62 days post-explosion with derived CO mass, temperature, and velocity; identification of dust continuum with determined dust temperature and mass; confirmation of SN 2024rbc as a Type Ib via spectral comparisons; estimates of $^{56}$Ni mass and ejecta mass from light curve fits; and insights into ejecta evolution and early dust formation processes in supernovae.
AI.conclusion: This study provides the first detection of CO in Type Ib SN ejecta and characterizes its physical properties along with dust characteristics, highlighting the role of Type Ib SNe in dust formation and contributing to understanding the chemical enrichment in the early Universe.

title: Derivation of the Kompaneets equation using the boost operator approach
comment: 26 pages, 2 figures, to be submitted to JCAP, comment welcome
summary: The repeated scattering of photons by thermal electrons at low temperatures is described by the Kompaneets equation and its generalized forms that include anisotropies and higher order temperature corrections. In this work, we use the boost operator approach to derive the related expressions in a transparent way that showcases the generality of the formalism and its application to radiative transfer problems. We consider the simplest form of the Kompaneets equation for the scattering in isotropic media at the leading order in the electron temperature and then include anisotropies in the photon field, reproducing previously obtained expressions for the evolution equations. For this we use expressions for the scattering operator in the electron rest frame up to first order in the electron recoil, O(h nu/m_e c^2), but then work at all orders in the electron momentum, p, as easily obtained with the boost operator approach. This shows how specific transformation rules can be formulated that allow simplification of the otherwise cumbersome and repetitive calculations. We also confirm the expressions for higher order temperature corrections in isotropic media, highlighting the validity of the approach presented here. As part of the derivation, we find expressions for the boost operator in general boost directions which we believe will also be useful in other applications of the formalism.

AI.tldr: This work uses boost operator techniques to systematically derive and generalize the Kompaneets equation describing photon scattering by thermal electrons, confirming known results and providing new formulas for anisotropies and higher order effects in a transparent and simplified manner.
AI.motivation: To provide a clear, general, and systematic approach to derive the Kompaneets equation and its generalizations for photon scattering by thermal electrons, including anisotropies and temperature corrections.
AI.method: Employing the boost operator formalism to derive the scattering operator expressions in the electron rest frame and transforming them to lab frame at all orders in electron momentum while including first order recoil effects; applying this to both isotropic and anisotropic photon fields.
AI.result: Recovered known evolution equations for Kompaneets-type scattering in isotropic and anisotropic media, confirmed higher order temperature corrections, derived general boost operator expressions for arbitrary directions, demonstrating simplifications and generality of the method.
AI.conclusion: The boost operator approach provides a transparent, systematic, and general framework for deriving Kompaneets and related scattering equations, simplifying calculations and enabling extensions to anisotropic and higher order temperature cases, with potential applications beyond the presented case.

title: RRAT J1541+4703: A Rotating Radio Transient Exhibiting Normal Pulsar States
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures, 2 Tables, Accept by ApJ
summary: Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs) are a class of pulsar-like objects characterized by intermittent radio emissions. Among them, RRATs that exhibit both RRAT and normal pulsar (NP) states may represent a key evolutionary stage from nulling pulsars to RRATs. We performed a detailed analysis of RRAT J1574+4703 using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST) at a frequency of 1250 MHz. Our findings indicate that this RRAT spends approximately 98% of its time in the RRAT state, with the remainder spent in an NP state exhibiting nulling behavior. Additionally, we observed distinct integral pulse profiles and polarization properties between the two states, suggesting that they originate from different emission heights and magnetospheric structures. Furthermore, it was observed that the NP states of this RRAT exhibit mode switching, with ~44% of the time spent in the normal mode and ~39% in the abnormal mode. Notably, abnormal modes are predominantly detected at the onset and termination of the NP states. This discrepancy between the modes indicates potential instability in the magnetospheric processes that govern the NP states.

AI.tldr: Observational study of RRAT J1574+4703 reveals it mostly emits as a RRAT but occasionally switches to a normal pulsar state with nulling and mode-switching, reflecting underlying magnetospheric changes and evolutionary significance.
AI.motivation: To investigate RRATs that exhibit both RRAT and normal pulsar states as potential key evolutionary stages between nulling pulsars and RRATs.
AI.method: Detailed observational analysis of RRAT J1574+4703 using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST) at 1250 MHz.
AI.result: RRAT J1574+4703 spends ~98% of its time in the RRAT state and the rest in an NP state with nulling behavior; distinct pulse profiles and polarization properties suggest different emission heights and magnetospheric structures. NP states show mode switching between normal (~44%) and abnormal (~39%) modes, with abnormal modes mainly at NP onset and termination indicating magnetospheric instability.
AI.conclusion: The dual-state behavior of RRAT J1574+4703 supports its role as an evolutionary link between nulling pulsars and RRATs, with different magnetospheric conditions driving its emission properties and instabilities during the NP states.

title: Investigating the radio emission in the Perseus cluster with LOFAR sub-80 MHz LBA
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 16 pages, 2 tables, 16 figures
summary: The Perseus cluster is a nearby cool-core galaxy cluster that hosts an archetypal radio mini-halo. Recent Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) High Band Antenna (HBA) observations at 120 - 168 MHz have revealed the presence of a giant radio halo within the cluster with a size of 1.1 Mpc enveloping the mini-halo. By exploring the spectral properties of the radio emission at low frequencies, we can gain deeper insights into the nature of this emission and improve our understanding of its origin. Here we present LOFAR Low Band Antenna (LBA) images of the cluster between 30.0 - 57.7 MHz, with a resolution of 19.2'' x 15.0'' and a r.m.s. noise of 3.7 mJy/beam . In our images, we detect both the mini-halo and giant radio halo. We measured the spectral indices between 44 and 144 MHz of the mini-halo and giant radio halo to be -1.34 +- 0.10, and -1.01 +- 0.11, respectively. An alternative and more direct measurement of the spectrum of the giant radio halo results in a spectral index of -1.28 +- 0.15. The discrepancy between both values is caused by the poor ionospheric conditions. In addition, we study two X-ray 'ghost cavities' in the cluster. These cavities are thought to have been produced by an older outburst from the central AGN 3C 84. We measure a spectral index between 44 and 144 MHz for the radio plasma in these cavities of -1.86 +- 0.12 and -1.90 +- 0.12 for the northwest and southern ghost cavities, respectively. Furthermore, by including VLA 352 MHz data, we find that the spectrum steepens at higher frequencies. These results are consistent with the ghost cavities being filled with old and aged radio plasma. We also detect the tailed radio galaxies NGC 1265 and IC 310. In our analysis, these sources show signs of spectral steepening along their tails.

AI.tldr: This paper presents LOFAR observations of the Perseus cluster revealing detailed spectral properties of its giant and mini radio halos and ghost cavities, showing aged plasma in cavities and spectral steepening in radio galaxy tails, enhancing understanding of cluster radio emission origins.
AI.motivation: The study aims to explore the spectral properties of radio emissions in the Perseus galaxy cluster to understand the origin and nature of its giant and mini radio halos and associated phenomena like ghost cavities.
AI.method: LOFAR Low Band Antenna observations between 30.0 - 57.7 MHz with high resolution and sensitivity were used to image the Perseus cluster, complemented by data from LOFAR High Band Antenna and VLA at higher frequencies; spectral indices were measured across these frequencies for different radio structures.
AI.result: Detection of both the mini-halo and giant radio halo with measured spectral indices of approximately -1.34 and -1.01 respectively, with some discrepancy due to ionospheric conditions; spectral indices for ghost cavities indicate aged radio plasma with steepening spectra at higher frequencies; detection of spectral steepening in tailed radio galaxies NGC 1265 and IC 310.
AI.conclusion: The spectral analyses support the characterization of the giant radio halo as an extended feature enveloping the mini-halo, and the identification of ghost cavities filled with old, aged radio plasma, consistent with prior AGN activity. Spectral steepening observed in radio tails further corroborates aging of synchrotron-emitting electrons along the tails.

title: The annular gap model under a rotating dipole field approximation: simulating gamma-ray light curve
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 1 Tables, Accept by ApJ
summary: A more realistic description of the magnetosphere is crucial for understanding the radiation emitted by pulsars. In this paper, we revisit the annular gap model by employing a rotating dipole field, which is more realistic than the static dipole field, as an approximation of the magnetic structure of the pulsar magnetosphere. Compared with the static dipole field approximation, the open field-line region, including both the core and annular gaps, is significantly enlarged, and the two regions become asymmetric with respect to the fiducial plane. We apply this model to three young gamma-ray pulsars with distinct light-curve morphologies, PSRs J0631$+$1036 (single peak), J1709$-$4429 (double peaks), and J1048$-$5832 (three peaks). Using viewing geometries constrained by radio polarization measurements, the annular gap model within the rotating dipole field successfully reproduces the main morphological features of their gamma-ray light curves above 0.1 GeV. Our model provides a framework for interpreting pulsar high-energy emission, which can be used to analyze the emission properties of high-energy pulsars.

AI.tldr: This paper improves pulsar magnetosphere modeling by using a rotating dipole field in the annular gap model, enlarging and asymmetrizing the open field-line region. It successfully reproduces gamma-ray light curves of three young pulsars, providing a robust framework for studying high-energy pulsar emissions.
AI.motivation: To achieve a more realistic description of the pulsar magnetosphere to better understand the radiation emitted by pulsars.
AI.method: Revisiting the annular gap model by employing a rotating dipole field approximation instead of a static dipole field to describe the magnetic structure of the pulsar magnetosphere.
AI.result: The open field-line region, including core and annular gaps, is significantly enlarged and becomes asymmetric. The model successfully reproduces the main morphological features of gamma-ray light curves for three young gamma-ray pulsars using viewing geometries constrained by radio polarization measurements.
AI.conclusion: The annular gap model with a rotating dipole field provides a realistic framework to interpret pulsar high-energy emission and analyze emission properties of high-energy pulsars.

title: Reducing cosmological degeneracies by combining multiple classes of LISA gravitational-wave standard sirens
comment: 7+2 pages, 3 figures
summary: We present the first joint gravitational-wave cosmological inference with LISA extreme mass-ratio inspirals at $z\lesssim1$ (galaxy redshifts) and massive black hole binaries at $z\gtrsim1$ (electromagnetic counterparts). Combining these standard sirens reduces cosmological degeneracies and yields competitive constraints on the Hubble constant $H_0$ and the dark-energy equation-of-state parameter $w_0$. This highlights LISA's potential for late-time cosmology across a broad redshift range with systematics distinct from electromagnetic distance indicators.

AI.tldr: This study combines LISA gravitational-wave observations from different source types across various redshifts to constrain cosmological parameters like the Hubble constant and dark energy properties, offering a novel and competitive approach to late-time cosmology.
AI.motivation: To improve cosmological parameter estimation by combining complementary gravitational-wave signals from different sources observed by LISA, thereby overcoming limitations of each individual probe and providing an independent cosmological measurement distinct from traditional electromagnetic methods.
AI.method: Joint cosmological inference using gravitational-wave standard sirens from LISA, specifically exploiting extreme mass-ratio inspirals at low redshifts and massive black hole binaries with electromagnetic counterparts at higher redshifts to break cosmological parameter degeneracies.
AI.result: The combined use of LISA standard sirens spanning a broad redshift range successfully reduces cosmological degeneracies and yields competitive constraints on key parameters including the Hubble constant and dark-energy equation-of-state parameter, illustrating LISA's promise for cosmology.
AI.conclusion: Combining LISA observations of extreme mass-ratio inspirals and massive black hole binaries provides competitive and robust constraints on cosmological parameters such as the Hubble constant and dark-energy equation-of-state, demonstrating LISA's strong potential in late-time cosmology.

title: Unifying the X-ray coronae and ultra-fast outflows: a PBI-enhanced outflow-based corona model for the inner accretion disc
comment: accepted by MNRAS, 14 pages, 7 figures
summary: The fact that luminous X-ray coronae and Ultra-Fast Outflows (UFOs) are both inferred to originate from the innermost regions of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) suggests a deep physical connection between them. However, standard magnetic buoyancy models struggle to transport sufficient energy through the radiation-pressure-dominated inner disc to sustain both the phenomena, creating a theoretical energy deficit. In this work, we propose an outflow-based model with energy transport enhanced by the Photon Bubble Instability (PBI) in the inner region. By coupling this enhanced energy supply with the MHD turbulence-driven mass-loading mechanism appropriate for weakly magnetized standard discs, we solve the dynamical and thermodynamic structure of the corona. We find that the model can successfully launch high speed winds matching observed UFO kinematics provided the mechanical acceleration efficiency is high ($f_{\rm acc}\gtrsim 0.5$). Furthermore, the model naturally reproduces the observed spectral evolution found in AGN coronae: as the accretion rate increases, the corona becomes optically thicker and cooler and produces a softer spectrum. Our results support an extended slab-like coronal geometry and suggest that UFOs and X-ray coronae in the inner discs are manifestations of the same magnetic activity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel model enhancing energy transport in AGN inner discs through photon bubble instability, unifying the origin of ultra-fast outflows and X-ray coronae as manifestations of the same magnetic processes, and it matches observed properties including UFO speeds and corona spectral changes with accretion rate.
AI.motivation: Standard magnetic buoyancy models fail to supply enough energy through radiation-pressure-dominated inner discs to explain the coexistence of luminous X-ray coronae and UFOs, indicating a theoretical energy deficit requiring a new approach.
AI.method: The study combines enhanced energy transport via Photon Bubble Instability with MHD turbulence-driven mass-loading to solve for the corona's dynamical and thermodynamic structure, matching observed UFO kinematics and spectral evolution.
AI.result: The model successfully reproduces observed UFO velocities when mechanical acceleration efficiency is high and explains the spectral softening and cooling of AGN coronae with increasing accretion rate, supporting an extended slab-like coronal geometry and a unified mechanism for UFOs and X-ray coronae.
AI.conclusion: The proposed outflow-based model with photon bubble instability effectively explains both luminous X-ray coronae and ultra-fast outflows in AGNs, linking them as results of the same magnetic activity in the inner accretion disc.

title: A velocity-dependent two-scale model for cosmic string networks with small-scale structure
comment: 15 poages, 3 figures
summary: We develop a semi-analytical model to describe the cosmological evolution of networks of cosmic strings with small-scale structure, by extending the velocity-dependent one-scale model to include an additional lengthscale describing the typical interkink density. We study the impact of the different physical processes involved in the production and removal of small-scale structure from cosmic strings on the attainment of a full linear scaling regime, in which the characteristic lengths of the network and of small-scale structure evolve proportionally to physical time and the root-mean-squared velocity of the network remains constant. We find, using this novel velocity-dependent two-scale model, that quite generally small-scale structure does not prevent the attainment of a linear scaling regime since, even if not enough kinks are carried away when loops are chopped from the network, gravitational backreaction is generally enough to ensure that the interkink density scales. We find, however, that this regime is characterized by a smaller energy density and root-mean-squared velocity when compared to strings without small-scale structure and that this reduction may be significant when scaling is maintained by gravitational backreaction. In this case, we also find that, before reaching full scaling, the network should evolve in a transient quasi-scaling regime, in which its evolution is very similar to that of cosmic strings without small-scale structure.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an extended velocity-dependent two-scale model that includes small-scale structures on cosmic strings, demonstrating that such structures do not prevent linear scaling due to gravitational backreaction, though they reduce energy density and velocity in the network.
AI.motivation: To understand how small-scale structure on cosmic strings affects their cosmological evolution, particularly the attainment of the linear scaling regime, which is critical for the theoretical and observational study of cosmic string networks.
AI.method: The paper develops a semi-analytical velocity-dependent two-scale model by extending the velocity-dependent one-scale model. This model incorporates an additional lengthscale to capture the typical interkink density, enabling examination of the production and removal processes of small-scale structure on cosmic strings.
AI.result: The model shows that despite the presence of small-scale structure, linear scaling regimes can be attained because gravitational backreaction compensates for insufficient kink removal via loop chopping. However, these regimes exhibit lower energy densities and velocities, with a significant reduction when gravitational backreaction dominates. The network also passes through a transient quasi-scaling phase resembling evolution without small-scale structure prior to full scaling.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that small-scale structure on cosmic strings does not prevent the network from achieving a linear scaling regime, though it results in a reduced energy density and root-mean-squared velocity compared to strings without such structure. Gravitational backreaction plays a crucial role in ensuring the interkink density scales appropriately, and before full scaling is reached, the network undergoes a transient quasi-scaling regime.

title: Simultaneous Multi-band Optical Follow-up Observations of a Gamma-Ray Flare in BL Lacertae
summary: On $2024$ October $5$, BL Lacertae ($2200+420$) experienced one of its brightest gamma-ray flares. We conducted simultaneous follow-up observations in the $u$, $v$, $g$, $r$, $i$, and $z$ bands from $2024$ October $17$ to November $21$ using the Mephisto telescope and its two $50$ cm twin auxiliary photometric telescopes of Yunnan University. Intraday variability (IDV) was detected in the $g$, $r$, $i$, and $z$ bands. The IDV duty cycle increased with observing frequency across these bands. The shortest variability time-scale, derived from auto-correlation analysis, constrains the upper limit of the black hole mass to be $M_{\bullet} \lesssim 10^{8.29} M_{\odot}$ assuming a Kerr black hole, and $M_{\bullet} \lesssim 10^{8.77} M_{\odot}$ assuming a Schwarzschild black hole. The emission region responsible for the observed variability has a size of $R \le 3.51 \times 10^{14}$ cm and is located at a distance of $R_H \le 2.83 \times 10^{15}$ cm from the central supermassive black hole. This distance is approximately three orders of magnitude smaller than the typical radius of the broad-line region, indicating that the emission region lies well within it. A general bluer-when-brighter (BWB) trend was detected on intraday time-scales, suggesting that shock-accelerated relativistic electrons enhance the high-energy particle population, leading to spectral hardening. A potential quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) with a period of $\sim 100.77$ minutes was detected with $>99.99$ per cent confidence, consistent with predictions from the magnetic reconnection model. These observed optical intraday variabilities and colour variations of BL Lacertae can be well explained by the turbulent jet model.

AI.tldr: Following a major gamma-ray flare in 2024, detailed multi-band optical monitoring of BL Lacertae revealed intraday variability and spectral hardening consistent with shock-accelerated electrons in a turbulent jet, constraining black hole mass and emission region parameters, and detecting a strong quasi-periodic oscillation likely due to magnetic reconnection.
AI.motivation: To investigate the optical intraday variability characteristics and emission region properties of BL Lacertae following a major gamma-ray flare on 2024 October 5.
AI.method: Simultaneous multi-band photometric observations using Mephisto and twin auxiliary telescopes were conducted, with data analyzed through auto-correlation and statistical methods to detect variability, spectral trends, and quasi-periodic oscillations.
AI.result: Identification of significant intraday variability increasing with frequency, constraints on black hole mass and emission region size/location within the broad-line region, clear bluer-when-brighter trend, and detection of a >99.99% confidence quasi-periodic oscillation around 100.77 minutes period consistent with magnetic reconnection models.
AI.conclusion: The intraday variability and color variations of BL Lacertae observed in multiple optical bands can be explained by the turbulent jet model, supported by the detection of a bluer-when-brighter trend and a quasi-periodic oscillation consistent with magnetic reconnection.

title: Brightest Cluster Galaxy ellipticity as proxy for halo shape: Orientation bias, assembly bias, and potential selection effects in SZ-selected clusters
comment: 28 Pages, 22 Figures
summary: The orientation of triaxial galaxy clusters with respect to the line-of-sight is expected to be one of the prime sources of scatter and potential bias in optical observables (e.g., richness and weak-lensing signal) of galaxy clusters. In this work, we use the observed shape of the central Brightest Cluster Galaxy (BCG) as proxy for the orientation along the line-of-sight for clusters selected via the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) effect from the South Pole Telescope (SPT) and Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) surveys, matched to optically selected clusters from the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 (DES). We construct two samples of clusters that are designed to be identical in SZ mass estimate and redshift but with the roundest vs. the most elliptical BCGs, which we expect to correspond to BCGs (and clusters) with major axes aligned along the line-of-sight vs. in the plane of the sky, respectively. We find that the optical richness of round-BCG clusters is $\sim 10$\% larger than that of elliptical-BCG clusters, in agreement with the expectation from projection effects and presenting the first such detection in data. The density profiles, however, are not in agreement with the expectation from projection effects: the 1-halo term (below $6~h^{-1}\rm{Mpc}$) of both the weak-lensing and galaxy density profiles are the same for the subsamples, contrary to previous studies based on X-ray selected clusters. In the 2-halo regime (above $6~h^{-1}\rm{Mpc}$), we find a significant excess of the elliptical-BCG cluster profiles compared to the round-BCG cluster profiles, which is the opposite of the expectation from numerical simulations. We hypothesize that the intrinsic shape of the BCG reflects not just the orientation angle, but also intrinsic properties of the cluster which can affect both the SZ signal and the amplitude of the 2-halo term.

AI.tldr: This study uses BCG shapes to probe galaxy cluster orientation effects on optical observables, finding that while richness increases with line-of-sight alignment as expected, weak-lensing and large-scale galaxy density profiles behave unexpectedly, indicating BCG shape encodes more than just orientation.
AI.motivation: To understand how the orientation of triaxial galaxy clusters along the line-of-sight affects optical observables such as richness and weak-lensing signal, since such orientation introduces scatter and bias in these measurements.
AI.method: Use the observed shape of the Brightest Cluster Galaxy (BCG) as a proxy for cluster orientation along the line-of-sight for clusters selected via the SZ effect from SPT and ACT surveys, matched to DES Year 3 optical clusters. Construct two cluster samples with matched SZ mass and redshift but differing BCG ellipticity to contrast properties of clusters aligned along the line-of-sight versus in the plane of the sky.
AI.result: Found that clusters with round BCGs (aligned along the line-of-sight) have ~10% higher optical richness than elliptical BCG clusters, confirming projection effect expectations. However, the 1-halo term weak-lensing and galaxy density profiles show no difference between subsamples, unlike previous X-ray studies. In the 2-halo regime, elliptical BCG clusters exhibit higher density than round BCG clusters, opposite to simulation predictions. This suggests BCG shape encodes not only orientation but also intrinsic cluster properties affecting both SZ signal and 2-halo term amplitude.
AI.conclusion: The BCG shape serves as a partial proxy for cluster orientation, influencing optical richness via projection effects, but also reflects intrinsic cluster properties that modulate SZ signals and large-scale density profiles, complicating simple interpretations based solely on orientation.

title: Core-Collapse Supernovae and their Gravitational Wave Signals: The Status of Theory and Modeling
comment: 31 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to Classical and Quantum Gravity as an inivited review for the focus issue "Core Collapse Supernova Gravitational Wave Theory and Detection: Past Present and Future". Comments welcome
summary: The detection of gravitational waves from a core-collapse supernova in the Milky Way or its vicinity represents a unique opportunity to probe the inner workings of these explosions. In this review, I briefly summarize our current understanding of the supernova explosion mechanism and then outline the physical processes that shape the supernova gravitational wave signal. The review highlights how the various components of the signal have the potential to constrain the progenitor rotation, the proto-neutron star structure, the nuclear equation of state, the nature of hydrodynamic instabilities, and the violence of turbulent motions in the supernova core. I also highlight some open questions and uncertainties in the theory of supernova gravitational wave astronomy as well as challenges for further progress. Specifically, there is a need to develop large model databases, systematic uncertainty quantification and methods for evidence assessment to prepare for multi-messenger observations from a Galactic supernova.

AI.tldr: This review discusses how gravitational waves from core-collapse supernovae can reveal details of the explosion mechanism and core physics, emphasizing current knowledge, open challenges, and the need for advanced modeling to enable effective interpretation of future observations.
AI.motivation: Detecting gravitational waves from core-collapse supernovae offers a unique way to understand their explosion mechanisms and internal dynamics.
AI.method: The paper reviews current theoretical understanding of supernova explosion physics and the resulting gravitational wave signals, discussing physical processes influencing these signals and how they relate to various astrophysical parameters.
AI.result: Highlights potential constraints gravitational wave signals can place on progenitor rotation, neutron star structure, nuclear equation of state, hydrodynamic instabilities, and turbulent core motions. Identifies open questions and challenges such as the need for large simulation databases, uncertainty quantification, and evidence assessment methods.
AI.conclusion: Gravitational wave observations from core-collapse supernovae can provide critical insights into the explosion mechanism and core dynamics, but progress requires improved modeling efforts and handling of uncertainties to fully exploit future multi-messenger data.

title: Perturbative and numerical study of nonlinear relativistic effects in weak lensing
comment: 50 pages, 8 figures. Code available on GitHub
summary: The standard weak lensing formalism assumes that the lensing map relating the observed image of a source to its intrinsic shape depends only on the deflection angle. We show that this description is incomplete beyond linear perturbation theory, even when only scalar perturbations are present at first order. Using the Jacobi map formalism, we derive expressions for the rotation field, shear B-modes, and their angular power spectra at second order in relativistic perturbation theory. In the standard formalism, rotation and shear B-modes share the same spectrum, however, this degeneracy is broken once the parallel transport of the Sachs basis is consistently taken into account. We quantify this correction numerically, finding a difference of about $5\%$ on large angular scales $\ell \sim 5$ for sources at redshift $z_\mathrm{s} = 0.5$. We also investigate frame-dragging effects, which are usually neglected in weak lensing. We present the first analytical derivation of the corresponding impact on the angular power spectrum of shear B-modes and show that it becomes the dominant contribution on scales $\ell \lesssim 10$. While both Sachs-basis rotation and frame dragging significantly affect shear B-modes on large scales, their effect on the observed galaxy ellipticity is of order $1\%$, making these nonlinear relativistic corrections challenging to detect in practice. Our results are supported by relativistic simulations of weak lensing observables, including the first numerical study of frame dragging in the power spectra of the lensing convergence and cosmic shear.

AI.tldr: This paper improves the weak lensing formalism beyond linear theory by deriving second-order corrections for rotation and shear B-modes, revealing new effects from parallel transport and frame dragging that alter power spectra on large scales, though their practical detectability is limited.
AI.motivation: The standard weak lensing formalism is incomplete beyond linear perturbation theory, necessitating a more accurate description including higher-order effects and relativistic corrections.
AI.method: Using the Jacobi map formalism, the authors derive second-order expressions for rotation field, shear B-modes, and their angular power spectra accounting for parallel transport of the Sachs basis and frame-dragging effects; they support their theoretical results with relativistic numerical simulations.
AI.result: They find that the degeneracy between rotation and shear B-modes spectra is broken by parallel transport corrections, with a 5% difference at large scales; frame-dragging effects dominate shear B-modes on very large scales and both effects impact ellipticity at the ~1% level, making detection challenging but important for precision cosmology.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear relativistic corrections, including Sachs-basis rotation and frame dragging, significantly affect weak lensing shear B-modes on large angular scales, breaking previous degeneracies and altering power spectra, although their observational impact on galaxy ellipticity remains small.

title: Derivation of the injection spectrum of positrons and electrons from Geminga and Monogem
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures
summary:
Extended $γ$-ray emission has been observed around several nearby pulsars and interpreted as inverse Compton radiation from relativistic electrons and positrons diffusing in the surrounding interstellar medium. In this work, we present a unified analysis of the TeV halos associated with the Geminga and Monogem pulsars, combining GeV--TeV $γ$-ray observations within a common physical framework.
  Assuming continuous injection of $e^\pm$ pairs from pulsar wind nebulae, we model the resulting $γ$-ray emission by accounting for particle diffusion and radiative energy losses. We find that the observed spectra of both Geminga and Monogem are well reproduced by the model, provided that particle transport in the vicinity of the pulsars is significantly suppressed with respect to the average Galactic diffusion. The injection spectra require cutoff energies of several tens of TeV, consistent with efficient acceleration in pulsar wind nebulae.
  Using the best-fit models inferred from the $γ$-ray data, we also evaluate the contribution of Geminga and Monogem to the local cosmic-ray positron flux measured by AMS-02. We find that the suppressed diffusion around the sources strongly limits the positron flux reaching the Earth, resulting in a subdominant contribution over the entire energy range probed by the experiment excect for the highest energy at around 1 TeV.
  Our results support an interpretation in which TeV halos trace regions of inhibited particle diffusion around pulsars, without implying a significant impact on the local cosmic-ray positron spectrum. This combined analysis highlights the importance of extended $γ$-ray observations for constraining particle transport in the vicinity of Galactic cosmic-ray sources.

AI.tldr: This study models gamma-ray emission from Geminga and Monogem pulsars, finding suppressed particle diffusion around them that limits their contribution to local cosmic-ray positrons, emphasizing gamma-ray observations as key to understanding cosmic-ray transport.
AI.motivation: To understand the nature of extended gamma-ray emission around nearby pulsars and its implications for particle transport and cosmic-ray positron flux near Earth.
AI.method: Unified modeling of gamma-ray emission from Geminga and Monogem TeV halos, incorporating continuous e± injection, particle diffusion, and radiative losses, fitted to GeV-TeV gamma-ray data.
AI.result: The model reproduces observed spectra assuming suppressed diffusion near pulsars and requires injection cutoff energies of several tens of TeV. The constrained diffusion strongly limits positron flux contribution to Earth, making it subdominant except near 1 TeV.
AI.conclusion: TeV halos represent regions of inhibited particle diffusion around pulsars without significantly affecting local cosmic-ray positron spectrum; extended gamma-ray observations are crucial for probing particle transport near Galactic cosmic-ray sources.

title: Impact of Antenna Structure and Orientation on Forward-Modelled Global 21 cm Signal Recovery
comment: 11 Pages, 9 Figures
summary: The redshifted 21 cm absorption trough from cosmic atomic hydrogen is one of the most promising probes of the early Universe, but its detection is challenged by bright foregrounds and instrumental systematics. In this work we quantify the impact of antenna mismodelling on signal recovery within a fully Bayesian, forward-modelled data analysis pipeline. We show that discrepancies between simulated and modelled antenna beams lead to frequency dependent errors in antenna temperature that can bias parameter inference. In particular, we demonstrate that orientation mismatches at the level of 0.25 degrees can significantly bias recovered signal parameters in typical observing scenarios. However, we also show that Bayesian evidence can be used to infer antenna orientation within this precision by scanning over model realisations. For structural mismodelling, we find that broadband recovery of all signal parameters requires accurate beam knowledge, but that partial recovery remains possible. Signal frequency and width can be robustly recovered under restricted frequency bands even when the antenna structure is imperfectly modelled, but signal depth is highly sensitive to beam errors. These results quantify the level of beam knowledge required for forward-modelled global 21 cm experiments and highlight the importance of observing strategy and antenna design in mitigating beam-sky coupling systematics.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies how inaccuracies in antenna beam modelling affect the recovery of the redshifted 21 cm absorption signal. Using Bayesian methods, it shows small orientation errors cause significant biases, but Bayesian evidence can correct these. Accurate beam knowledge is crucial for full signal recovery, though frequency and width parameters are more robust to errors than signal depth.
AI.motivation: The study addresses the challenge of detecting the redshifted 21 cm absorption signal from cosmic atomic hydrogen, which is impeded by bright foregrounds and instrumental systematics, particularly antenna mismodelling errors.
AI.method: A fully Bayesian, forward-modelled data analysis pipeline is used to quantify the impact of antenna beam mismodelling on signal recovery and parameter inference. The approach includes simulating antenna beams and comparing them with modelled beams, and scanning over model realizations to infer antenna orientation using Bayesian evidence.
AI.result: Even small antenna orientation mismatches (0.25 degrees) can significantly bias recovered signal parameters. Bayesian evidence can precisely infer antenna orientation to mitigate this bias. Structural mismodelling affects broadband recovery of all signal parameters, but signal frequency and width can still be robustly recovered in restricted frequency bands despite imperfect antenna modelling. Signal depth, however, remains highly sensitive to beam errors.
AI.conclusion: Accurate knowledge of antenna beams is critical for forward-modelled global 21 cm experiments to avoid biases in signal recovery. Observing strategy and antenna design play essential roles in mitigating beam-sky coupling systematics and ensuring reliable parameter inference.

title: Multi-mission Investigation of X-ray Superorbital Modulation in the Supergiant High Mass X-ray Binary 4U 1538-52
comment: 21 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Superorbital modulations has been detected in the supergiant High-Mass X-ray binary 4U 1538-52 using long-term monitoring with the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory Burst Alert Telescope (BAT). The source also exhibits a long-term pulse period evolution as seen with Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE), INTEGRAL, and Fermi Gamma-Ray Burst Monitor (GBM) that appears uncorrelated with changes in its X-ray flux. To investigate the mechanisms causing these superorbital modulations and its possible dependence on pulse period changes, we analyzed long-term monitoring with Swift-BAT and Monitor of All Sky X-ray Image Gas Slit Camera (MAXI-GSC) to construct dynamic power spectra and superorbital intensity profiles. In addition, we used pointed X-ray observations from Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR) and Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer mission (NICER) to investigate the pulsation and spectral properties across different superorbital and orbital phase intervals. We find the presence of superorbital modulations in the MAXI-GSC 2-20 keV lightcurves, consistent with the periodicity observed with the Swift-BAT lightcurves. However, no significant changes are detected in the pulse profiles or spectral parameters across different superorbital, orbital, or pulse-change intervals. This lack of spectral or timing variations with orbital and superorbital phases suggests that the mechanisms driving the observed superorbital modulation and pulse period changes are likely associated with large-scale stellar wind structures, such as Co-Rotating Interaction regions, within the stellar wind of the supergiant companion.

AI.tldr: This study confirms superorbital modulations in 4U 1538-52 and attributes them, along with pulse period changes, to large-scale stellar wind structures, with no significant spectral or timing changes detected across phases.
AI.motivation: Investigate the mechanisms behind detected superorbital modulations in 4U 1538-52 and their relation to pulse period changes.
AI.method: Analyzed long-term X-ray monitoring data from Swift-BAT and MAXI-GSC to construct dynamic power spectra and intensity profiles; used NuSTAR and NICER pointed observations to study pulsation and spectral properties across superorbital and orbital phases.
AI.result: Detected superorbital modulations consistent across instruments, but found no significant changes in pulse profiles or spectral parameters across phases or pulse-change intervals.
AI.conclusion: The absence of spectral or timing variations suggests that superorbital modulation and pulse period changes are driven by large-scale stellar wind structures, such as Co-Rotating Interaction Regions in the supergiant companion's stellar wind.

title: Probing Interacting Dark Sectors with upcoming Post-Reionization and Galaxy Surveys
comment: 12 pages, 6 sets of figures, 11 tables
summary: We investigate the constraining power of future post-reionization and galaxy surveys on possible interactions between dynamical dark energy and dark matter. The analysis focuses on the interaction strength and the dark energy equation of state parameters, in addition to the six standard cosmological parameters. Using fiducial values obtained from the current observational bounds (Planck 2018 + DESI DR2 + Pantheon+), mock datasets for upcoming 21-cm intensity mapping, galaxy clustering and cosmic shear observations from the SKA-mid, and for the upcoming large-scale survey from the Euclid mission, were generated. Subsequently, Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses combining current cosmological data with these mock datasets were performed to forecast parameter constraints. The results indicate that both SKA-mid and Euclid observations can significantly improve constraints on interacting dark sector parameters. In particular, the interaction strength and dark energy equation of state parameters can be constrained considerably tighter than current combined constraints from Planck 2018, DESI DR2 and Pantheon+. Comparing different probe combinations and survey configurations, it is found that SKA2 provides the tightest projected constraints, particularly on the interaction strength, while Euclid achieves a precision broadly comparable to that of SKA1. The results highlight the potential of these upcoming surveys to probe interactions within the dark sector.

AI.tldr: Future surveys like SKA and Euclid can greatly enhance constraints on dark energy-dark matter interactions, providing more precise cosmological parameter measurements than current data allows.
AI.motivation: To explore how future post-reionization and galaxy surveys can better constrain the interactions between dynamical dark energy and dark matter, beyond current observational limits.
AI.method: Generation of mock datasets based on fiducial parameters from current cosmological observations (Planck 2018, DESI DR2, Pantheon+), simulating 21-cm intensity mapping, galaxy clustering, and cosmic shear from SKA-mid and Euclid surveys, followed by Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses to forecast parameter constraints.
AI.result: Both SKA-mid and Euclid surveys can substantially tighten constraints on the interaction strength between dark energy and dark matter and on dark energy equation of state parameters, surpassing current combined data limitations; specifically, SKA2 offers the strongest projected constraints, especially on interaction strength, while Euclid achieves precision comparable to SKA1.
AI.conclusion: Upcoming large-scale surveys such as SKA and Euclid hold significant potential to improve understanding and measurement of dark sector interactions, enabling more precise cosmological parameter estimation than currently possible.

title: Dynamical Systems in Cosmology: Reviewing An Alternative Approach
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures. Article for the Philosophical Transactions A Issue Dynamical Systems and Stability in Cosmology and Gravitation
summary: Dark energy is one of the deepest puzzles in modern cosmology, and mounting evidence suggests that it is not just a cosmological constant but a genuinely dynamical component. Although cosmology and dynamical systems theory emerged from different disciplines, dynamical systems methods have become essential tools to uncover the qualitative evolution of the universe. The equations governing homogeneous and isotropic cosmologies can be naturally written as systems of ordinary differential equations, making them an ideal arena for dynamical system analysis. This review begins with a sharp, streamlined introduction to the standard dynamical systems toolkit widely used in cosmology. We then move on to alternative formulations based on polar and hyperbolic variable transformations. These approaches unlock powerful new ways to probe a broad spectrum of scalar field dark energy models, to set and constrain initial conditions, and to analyze tracking behavior across wide classes of potentials. The review is self-contained, but consistently directs the reader to more specialized and in-depth treatments where needed.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews dynamical systems approaches to cosmology, focusing on standard methods and novel variable transformations that enable deep analysis of scalar field dark energy models and their evolution.
AI.motivation: To address the puzzle of dark energy being a dynamical component in cosmology and to utilize dynamical systems methods to understand the qualitative evolution of the universe.
AI.method: Review and introduction of standard and alternative dynamical systems tools, including polar and hyperbolic variable transformations, applied to homogeneous and isotropic cosmologies modeled as systems of ordinary differential equations.
AI.result: Presentation of powerful new approaches for analyzing a broad spectrum of scalar field dark energy models, initial conditions, and tracking behavior across various potential classes, offering both a streamlined toolkit and references to specialized literature.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical systems methods, enhanced by alternative variable transformations, provide essential, versatile tools for probing the dynamics of dark energy in cosmology, facilitating better understanding and constraints on scalar field models.

title: From friction scaling to an efficient method for estimating bubble wall velocity
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures
summary: We present a unified description of first-order cosmological phase transition dynamics that links the phenomenological friction model employed in hydrodynamic simulations to the microscopic treatment based on Boltzmann equations. We derive an approximate analytical expression for the chemical potential and demonstrate that the resulting friction parameter $\tildeη$ follows a simple power-law dependence on the transition strength ($\propto v_n^4/T_n^4$). Incorporating this scaling into a phenomenological framework accurately reproduces the terminal wall velocities obtained from the full microscopic analysis performed using \texttt{WallGo}. This approach offers an efficient method to quantify out-of-equilibrium contributions to friction and reliably estimate bubble-wall velocities.

AI.tldr: This paper unifies phenomenological and microscopic friction models in cosmological phase transitions, deriving a power-law scaling for friction that accurately predicts bubble-wall velocities.
AI.motivation: To unify phenomenological and microscopic descriptions of friction in first-order cosmological phase transitions and improve the accuracy of bubble-wall velocity predictions.
AI.method: Derivation of an approximate analytical expression for the chemical potential linking friction parameters to transition strength, and validation through hydrodynamic simulation frameworks and microscopic Boltzmann equation analysis using WallGo.
AI.result: Obtained a power-law scaling for the friction parameter with transition strength, enabling accurate reproduction of terminal wall velocities from microscopic simulations within a phenomenological model.
AI.conclusion: The unified framework efficiently quantifies out-of-equilibrium friction effects and reliably estimates bubble-wall velocities in cosmological phase transitions.
